utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kapetina. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Good morning, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Amelia Mattis, who is from the Thomas Jefferson Law School in San Diego and has been with my team since May of this year. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kapetina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you to pause between our exchanges and also that we both speak slowly, and we shall thus lose less time and avoid correcting the transcript. Mr. Kapetina, I'd like to ask you if you have given a statement to my Defence team.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please have 1D9168 in e-court. Please pay attention. We have versions in B/C/S, both versions. Can you see the statement on the screen in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. However, I have a correction. There was a slight error under item 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you have read the statement and signed it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please wait for the interpretation to conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown the last page so that he can identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature, Mr. Kapetina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Everything that you told my Defence team, was that faithfully reflected in the statement, and do you need to make any corrections?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes. I said under item 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please have page 4, or it may be even 3.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: The beginning of the sentence should not read "May" but "March." That's the only mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That has been recorded. As for the remainder of your statement, does it truthfully reflect what you told the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today as the ones put to you by the team, would your answers essentially be the same?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender this statement and the associated exhibits into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: A few, actually, Your Honour, and a couple of observations. The -- there have been associated exhibits removed from the 92 -- from the final statement that were included in the 92 ter notification, so I can go through those or Dr. Karadzic can. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just pausing there. Mr. Karadzic, I take it that you are tendering four items of associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellencies, four of them, and I would like them to be added to our 65 ter list. There's a fifth one which I will probably have to lead live, which is a manual drafted by Mr. Kapetina for emergency situations, however it hasn't been translated and I will have to discuss it with him. As for the others have already been admitted under either P or D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will express the Chamber's view first, Ms. Edgerton. Among them, Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber is of the view that two of the items not forming an indispensable and inseparable part of the statement. They are 1D9736, referred to in paragraph 19; and 1D9738, referred to in paragraph 30. Without them the statement can be understood without any difficulty. So if you need to tender them, you should lead them live with the witness, as well as showing the relevance of the documents. Otherwise, do you have any objection with respect to the two remaining items, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive the statement as well as two associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 92 ter statement 1D9168 will be D3856. 10643 will be Exhibit D3857, and 30076 will be Exhibit D3858.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm going now to read a summary of Mr. Dragan Kapetina's statement in English. [In English] From 1985, Dragan Kapetina worked at the republic secretariat for the national defence, later the ministry of defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In 1990, before the multi-party elections, he was appointed chief republican defence inspector of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He remained in this post until the end of March 1992. After May 1992, he did specialist work at the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska. In March 1995, he was appointed secretary of the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska. As the chief republican inspector, his duty was to oversee the implementation of the federal laws on national defence and to monitor the implementation of the republican laws. After the first multi-party elections in BH in 1990, the key posts in the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina were assigned to the Muslims and Croats. The HDZ candidate, Jerko Doko, became minister, and Kazim Begovic, a JNA colonel nominated by the SDA, became his deputy. Doko was Croat and Begovic was Muslim. This distribution of key positions in the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina prevented the Serbian personnel from performing their regular duties. During this period, the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina focused on taking over the powers of the federal organs in the sphere of defence, breaking up the JNA and transforming the Territorial Defence into the armed forces of the republic. All of these activities were in direct contravention with the provisions of the federal and republican constitutions. In May 1991, Minister of Defence Jerko Doko rejected the annual inspection programme presented by Dragan Kapetina because it was not reconcilable with Doko's task to break up the existing defence system. Dragan Kapetina expressed his concerns about the widespread and systematic violation of valid laws and drafted an official report to the government and the Presidency of B and H to warn them that they were exceeding their constitutional powers. When adopting decisions on the -- Mr. Kapetina's warnings at meetings of the government and the National Defence Council of B and H, the Serbian members were out-voted. Before the war, the Presidency of BH and the other state authorities, including the Ministry of Defence, were principally engaged in preventing Muslims and Croatian conscripts from BH from being sent to the JNA and in creating the core of the BH Army out of the Patriotic League, the Green Berets, the MUP reserve forces and Territorial Defence. Dragan Kapetina quit his job at the ministry in March 1992 and returned to his village in the municipality of Hadzici exclusively for security reasons. During the stay in his village, the political council of the Serbian municipality was established together with the Assembly of the Serbian people in Hadzici, and he was elected vice-president of the Assembly. The proclamation of the Serbian municipality of Hadzici was a measure taken to protect the Serbian people and preserve peace in the area. The newly established Assembly decided to fully respect all agreements made bit three people at the republican level with a view of resolving the crisis. As for the Muslim part of Hadzici municipality, the Muslim authorities took a number of tough measures against the Serbian population. On 30th of April, 1992, Dragan Kapetina drove his family to Serbia out of fear for their safety, but his parents remained in their family house, which was under the control of the Muslim authorities. His father was taken to the Silo concentration camp in Tarcin where he died in November 1992 due to the dreadful conditions and torture. On 10th of May, 1992, Mr. Kapetina resumed his work at the Ministry of Defence in Serbian Republic of B and H in Pale. The focus of his work was to develop two systemic laws, the Law of the Army and the Law of the Defence. In addition he worked on sub-laws and regulations on application of the International Law of War. In July 1995, Mr. Kapetina was called to the office of Mr. Karadzic, who wanted information about the situation in Srebrenica. Mr. Karadzic appeared very angry because he could not establish communication with the commander of the Main Staff, the Chief of the Main Staff, the Drina Corps, or the minister of defence, and he did not know what was happening in Srebrenica. And that would be short summary. I would now like to go through some documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just before we do that, and I realise the summary isn't evidence, Your Honour, but when Dr. Karadzic said that when adopting decisions on Mr. Kapetina's warnings at meetings of the government the Serbian members were out-voted, that's not the evidence of Mr. Kapetina. The evidence in paragraph 19 is that his warnings weren't discussed at the meeting. So Dr. Karadzic should be a bit careful in his summaries. Also, adding things to his summaries, for example, the ethnic background of Mr. Doko and Mr. Begovic, which is not in Mr. Kapetina's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please have 1D9736 in e-court. [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before Mr. Kapetina answers, I'm not receiving English interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apologies from the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are so many Serbs here that I believe that all of you have learned the Serbian language by now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you need to repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, can you tell us the name of the publication, the date of the publication, and in ethnic terms who the author of the article is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I can't see exactly the date. I'd say it was September 1991. Yes, 18th September 1991, and I think that the author of this article is a Bosniak, Zead Dernisevic [phoen]. I think he's a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What can you say about this statement that there was only one conscript from Livno? Can you tell us what is reflected in this article. And then there's another reference to you, Dragan Kapetina, the minister of defence, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes. The president of Bosnia-Herzegovina was preventing conscripts from going to serve in the JNA even though that was beyond the powers, constitutional powers, of the constitution, and we can see here that there was only one conscript from Livno, probably a Serb, his name was Maljkovic, and another 87 failed to respond, and then there was my written warning to the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina in which I cautioned the two highest government bodies that they were assuming the powers of federal organs and that they were operating beyond the powers that they have.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can see this middle paragraph in Serbian which makes reference to this five-hour meeting. Can you tell us who the participants are, and can you tell us their ethnicity? Can we enlarge in middle column. This sentence which starts "Inace..." This is the last paragraph. Can you just tell us the names and tell us who they are and what was the meeting about.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes. Representatives of the JNA held a meeting with members of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the promise was made that the conscripts who were being sent to serve in the army would not be dispatched to war zones but, rather, to trading centres that were far away from the then-war zones, for example, in Croatia at the time. And here we have representatives of the 5th Army and the commanders of all the corps deployed in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Vukosavljevic, commander of the Territorial Defence, Serbian, Muharem Fetahagic and Fikret Jakic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Commander of the Banja Luka and Tuzla Corps, and so on and so forth. And Jure Pelivan the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have page 3 so that we can see what Dragan Kapetina's assessment was. Already in September of 1991 you were issuing warnings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, the article's been read out. I was trying to find out what Mr. Kapetina said the meeting was about somewhere in the article, and I haven't been able to do that yet. We have no foundation with respect to the larger article itself, and I have no idea how this warning -- or we have no idea how this warning, which Mr. Kapetina hasn't commented on, relates to his written evidence. So I'd say there's insufficient foundation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could ask Mr. Kapetina how this meeting took place, what was the cause for convening it, and what was the participation of the Ministry of Defence of BH in trying to resolve those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that period --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Kapetina. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe he could ask Mr. Kapetina if he was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kapetina, you heard Ms. Edgerton's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't in the meeting held at the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This exhibit relates to paragraph 19. Mr. Kapetina, was your written paper and submission are made at the meeting, and did you have any contribution, not in physical sense, in these meetings and in these attempts to put things in order in terms of the law?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: This meeting described by the author did not contain -- did not contain my warning. It was held with representatives of -- representatives of JNA stationed in Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, my written warning to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that they were breaking the laws and the constitution, was discussed at the meeting of the National Defence Council chaired by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, the president of the Presidency. At this meeting the majority were Serbs. However, my warning was not discussed. Instead, quite simply, the president of the Presidency removed this warning from the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, I believe that this is within the official remit of Mr. Kapetina and is certainly a relevant one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3859, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Karadzic, I forgot to ask you one question -- ask one question about an associated exhibit. That is Variant A and B document, the 65 ter number of which is 10643. I told that I would admit it, but what it's point of tendering it separately, because we have that document in evidence. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't think it's necessary. I was going to suggest that we not admit that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll strike it off. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 1D9738. It is related to paragraph 30 in the statement of Mr. Kapetina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, do you know this document and what is it? The date, who issued it, and what is it about? Do you see the heading?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes. This is a brief about certain aspects of the political and security situation in the area of Hadzici municipality. I had some information that is covered in this brief, and I believe the author of this brief was my co-worker at the Ministry of Defence before he transferred to the command of the military district, Milan Atlagic. I didn't have the entire text, but I did have some knowledge about these events in Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the end of February 1992. That's the date of the referendum, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see page 2 in Serbian. Look at the penultimate paragraph where certain things are underlined. What is it about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes. The brief speaks about the arming drive, the distribution of light weapons, where they are stored, and that a certain Ahmet Budic, a reserve officer employed at the TAT enterprise is involved. There are rockets, rocket launchers for the zolja. Leaders of the Bosnia community in Hadzici were involved. I heard information about this but not exactly what is written here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I -- I miss again foundation, Your Honours. We don't know to what extent this information corresponds with what this witness might have heard. In fact, he said it's not exactly what's written here, and he has -- no. I think there's not been sufficient comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to paragraph 30, and could you tell us, although you've said it already, who is the author, and how is he related to you? Was he in the same service?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Milan Atlagic worked at the Ministry of Defence for four years in the security sector. Then he moved to the command of the military district but also -- but that was also part of the Ministry of Defence. He was my co-worker, and I received information like all the other senior staff at the ministry that related to security matters. I've said before that I did not receive this brief as such, but I knew most of these things and Atlagic had informed me. I didn't say otherwise. I even had more information. For instance, in that period the police in Hadzici seized a truck on Mount Igman full of light weaponry that was smuggled by the paramilitaries belonging to the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, Your Excellencies, that we have now enough foundation to admit this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3857, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 1D9735.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, in paragraph 7 of your statement, you talk about the manual for developing a contingency plan that you wrote in 1990. Were you shown the paper known as Variant A and Variant B, and what can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Before you answer, Mr. Kapetina. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Your Honours I'm sure are aware this is a document that the Prosecution objected to. It's a very lengthy document that was used with this witness during his previous testimony in the Krajisnik case some years ago and wasn't even translated at that time. There's not a page of this document that's been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow your objection. So you are objecting to putting this document to the witness at all?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because it is so large and it is untranslated. There's simply no way for us to even begin to think of dealing with this document when we're not able to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I can understand the Prosecution's position, but hopefully Dr. Karadzic will take the witness to a particular portion of this document that can be addressed and admitted if appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll consider whether we can admit it or not at the end of the examination. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 8 of this book. That's 9. Could we see the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, what is defined in this chapter? This is chapter 1. Could you describe to us in your own words what is said in this chapter?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: First of all, I authored this manual, and as chief republic inspector, it was my duty to inspect together with other inspectors contingency plans, and through this manual I tried to help those who made such contingency plans in Bosnia-Herzegovina to make them more easily. And those who made such plans was everybody from local authorities, local communes, businesses, socio-political organisations, even associations of citizens. Each one had the obligation to develop a contingency plan, and I wanted this manual to facilitate their work and to teach them how to make these plans. On this page I tried to define contingencies using, of course, the provisions of the Law on All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In line 24 what is missing is that the making of these plans was their duty. Did you say that it was their duty?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes, it was their legal obligation. All those who made contingency plans were legally obliged to do so in keeping with the Law on All People's Defence. Everybody had to develop a contingency plan for contingencies such as aggression, military aggression, or internal conflicts that involved the use of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you said a moment ago socio-political organisations were also an entity in the defence system, can you translate that into normal language? What are socio-political organisations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I'll try. In the previous system it was the League of Communists, The Socialist Alliance of Working People, The Socialist Alliance of Youth, and in the multi-party system it was the political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now read out the third paragraph from the top about the Law on All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: The Law on All People's Defence defines contingencies as follows: Other contingencies for the purpose of this law are understood to mean armed or other activity that directly jeopardises the independence of the country, its sovereignty, and territorial integrity, and the established social system under the constitution of SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the law defines contingencies.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we now see page 15. So this is the manual. What does this manual achieve? What do entities in the defence system have to do? Is this based on the law, and if they follow the manual, would they be complying with their legal obligations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: This entire segment of planning when we're talking about contingency plans envisages measures to prevent contingencies, that is preventive measures, to avoid contingencies, and then there is the repressive part aimed at eliminating contingencies once they occur. In addition to the law, there were also guidelines to eliminate contingencies and the decision on the methodology for the development of contingency plans. Those were federal regulations at the level of Yugoslavia, where as Bosnia-Herzegovina also had guidelines by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the development of contingency plans in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I was one of the authors and participants in the development of these guidelines. My manual was based on the republic law on the two federal regulations and one republic law on the development of contingency plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you read out the first paragraph from section 3, "Preventing contingencies from occurring..."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: "... all the way up to the adoption of guidelines to eliminate contingencies (19 July 1989) and the decision on the basis of a uniform methodology to develop contingency plans (24 November 1989) the tasks, measures, and procedures to prevent contingencies from occurring were established in the plans to prevent and eliminate contingencies."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was fast, but the interpreters managed. Can we now see page 23. The previous one. Section 3, The substance of contingency plans, these bullet points.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Under item 4 of the decision of the federal executive council, contingency plans shall contain an estimate of the political and security situation, i.e., assessment of the security situation. So everybody does this evaluation at their own level. Second bullet point: Tasks, measures, and procedures, organisation of forces and resources to eliminate contingencies in one's purview. And third bullet point: Measures of readiness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now see page 25. The entire page is important, but could you read out the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Instead of asking the witness to read out which was untranslated, why don't you ask the witness to -- ask the witness a question directly, not in a leading way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try, but this has not been translated, and we'll see how that will reflect on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, on this page we see some text about measures to eliminate contingencies. Can you tell us what is envisaged, which obligations does the law impose in the prevention and elimination of contingencies that we see in the last paragraph on this page?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I said at the beginning that this plan has a preventative nature aimed at preventing contingencies from occurring, and all entities are supposed to plan measures in keeping with the law. First of all, everybody is supposed to do their job in keeping with the constitution and the law to consistently enforce regulations, ensure co-ordination, co-operation. Simply comply with all their obligations in keeping with the constitution and the law, which prevents the occurrence of chaos, anarchy, and other things that could jeopardise peace and stability.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the last line it says in that sense one of the possible approaches in the development of documents to eliminate contingencies, what is this supposed to mean, document to eliminate contingencies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I had not seen this document for a long time because I didn't keep a single copy for my own use. I would need to see page 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may before the witness goes further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm really wondering what the relevance is of the very detailed evidence that we're hearing that I've had no notice of, as I've indicated, regarding this document from 1990.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this document preceded Variants A and B and the indictment bases many charges against me on the Serbian side on that. This is from 1990, not from 1995, because this is what laid the legal foundation for what followed. Papers A and B cannot be understood without this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you just tell us. You see the model of this paper here. The last paragraph, "Measures established in the guidelines on measures for readiness." Can you tell us what this is about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes, the Presidency of Yugoslavia issued a document entitled "Guidelines on Measures of Readiness," and there were three degrees involved, and all the planning entities in Yugoslavia were duty-bound to carry through these measures in order to prevent contingencies. That is to say so that there would not be any kind of armed intervention on other intervention so that this would be nipped in the bud as I've already explained, and I say here how entities are supposed to work this out on the basis of a table with clear tasks. Those who will carry them out, the way in which this will be carried out, and co-operation with other entities if so planned. So I've just given a model, an example of how this document -- or, rather, how this can be done in an easier manner and how it could be more user-friendly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that from line 6 -- ah, I see, that's the answer, yes. All right. Could we see the next page now. In line 16, that's not the question. That's part of the question. Ah, thank you. Yes. Now it's been corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please present item 4 to us now, the content and way plans are -- contingencies plans are elaborated at municipality level. Could you please read this out to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise, but this evidence is not in this witness's statement. This evidence is being presented in the context --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. When you're saying that it is not in the statement, means that detail is lacking. He referred to the manual, so to speak, in para 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. That's the only mention, only comment relating to this document in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I also noticed that Ms. Edgerton --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you put a pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton earlier stated that she had no notice that this document was going to be used, but in fact it's listed as an additional exhibit in our Rule 92 ter notice, and this is a partial Rule 92 ter witness so items can be led live which are not detailed in the statement which is what Dr. Karadzic is doing. It's unfortunate that the document is being translated and I -- is not translated and I realise it puts the Prosecution at a disadvantage, but I don't think that that's any bar to making whatever use of the document that can be made at this time, and the Prosecution can recall the witness or ask to recall the witness if later when the document is translated it finds that there were questions that it would have put and that it didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the issue is still the use of untranslated document, which is in particular lengthy and -- yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Of course we've had notice of this document. It was one the documents I indicated that we had in -- that I had initially objected to. It's not translated. This is a critical issue that we should have had notice of, and this detailed evidence is not in the witness's statement, and quite frankly, Your Honour, we shouldn't have to apply to recall this witness because we're prejudiced for the lack of translation of a document that's previously appeared before these Chambers -- before this Tribunal and not yet been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you expand further the fact that this appeared before the Chamber and had not yet been translated.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I misspoke. Not this Chamber, Your Honour. Another Chamber of this Tribunal in the Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was admitted in other Chambers?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll just check the admission status in the previous proceedings with Mr. Reid. That'll just take a couple of minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So when it was used in the other Chamber, the Prosecution should have been in the position to know about the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could just have your indulgence while Mr. Reid checks this I could respond to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Sladojevic has found the portion of the transcript of the Krajisnik case where this document was admitted which is admitted as D123 on page 20109, and also noted that Mr. Tieger cross-examined the witness in the Krajisnik case on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: About the translation at that proceedings? Do you have a clue?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I do. And thank you to Mr. Sladojevic. Four pages of that document were admitted which were translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you didn't have the time to compare the pages that were admitted in that case and those shown to the witness in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I didn't know that -- what pages were going to be shown to the witness in this case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So are you objecting to the last question?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And -- pardon me, it's D123 in the Krajisnik case rather than 1203, just to correct the record. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the question was how the contingency plans were elaborated at municipality level. Are you objecting to that question or not, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have had no notice that this detailed evidence was going to be presented today from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, the Chamber agrees that Defence notice was not a very kind one, but in light of the para 7, the Chamber has no difficulty with continuing with this evidence. The Chamber agrees with Mr. Robinson if necessary the Prosecution is entitled to recall this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. And just to correct the record in terms of this exhibit because I don't want to be misleading. This document was assigned D123 in the Krajisnik case at transcript page 20109. It was admitted -- portions of this document, said His Honour Judge Orie, were provisionally admitted awaiting translation and further specification, and that was repeated at transcript page 20110, D123 being provisionally admitted. And I was unable to be more accurate previously because I didn't have the pages in front of me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Probably you need to ask the question again, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, you told us who all the Defence entities were, and you mentioned socio-political communities which means municipalities, local communes, and republics in plain language. Can you tell us what the municipalities were charge of, and that is what item four deals with here.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: The plan for contingencies at municipal level contains an assessment of the political security situation in the municipality, then tasks, measures, and procedures, organisation, forces, and resources for the elimination of contingencies and measures of readiness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the next page, please. Let's not read it out. Can you just tell us what this assessment of the political security situation in the municipality pertains to.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Well, this assessment mostly speaks of the situation regarding the socio-political system, the work of state organs, the functioning of the economy, economic entities then social services, education, culture, and so on. That is to say, the overall situation with regard to political activities at the level of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have page 34 now. Can you present this chapter to us: Elaboration of plans.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes, this is the content of plans with regard to state organs, that is to say local government organs. The content is the same like for other planning entities. One starts from an assessment and then each organ gives an assessment within their own purview on the basis of law, and then of course they take measures to prevent contingencies and eliminate them once they've happened.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat his question? It is too fast for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 42 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't hear your question. Please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just asked for page 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this chapter 7 pertains to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: It speaks of the content and way in which these plans are elaborated at the level of local communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To what extent -- actually, what kind of correlation is there between this and the measures that are taken at the level of the municipality and the level of the entire federal state?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Practically the local commune was the basic cell of the society at the time, and this plan basically pertained to measures and tasks that would be implemented by citizens directly as entities of the system within the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us where socio-political organisations belong within this system? Was this before the multi-party system was introduced?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes. This manual was written before the multi-party system was introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the position and role of the ruling political party in the system of All People's Defence and the system of managing contingencies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Any political party, regardless of whether it is the ruling party or a party in the opposition, was duty-bound to have its own contingency plan, and these plans were mostly made at the level of the republic. The organ of that political party at republican level, that is. However, Municipal Boards and all local boards also had their own plans within that plan. So the party may have had these plans -- or, rather, did have these plans along the vertical line from the republican level all the way to the level of local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like you to remember papers A and B. That was shown to you in the -- in the Krajisnik case; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- or, rather, what is it that you can tell us about the foundation in law and the content of that paper?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Earlier on I said, and I'm saying again, that each and every party in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time and on the basis of the law and other bylaws that we refer to here, the guidelines of the Federal Executive Council and of the Presidency and so on. So each and every political party was duty-bound to elaborate its own contingency plan and adapt it to its own way of political organisation from top to bottom. I think that this document that was elaborated by the SDS that consists of Variant A and Variant B and two levels of readiness was done in a professional and lawful manner and that this was the obligation of the ruling party to have this kind of plan for this kind of situation which may occur and may threaten peace and other values of the system. And if there are no other questions, I can go on. I can tell you what it was that I observed in this instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this man was presented to us as a fact witness in his statement and in his 92 ter summary, and I don't think it's appropriate for Dr. Karadzic to take him in his questions outside of that, to have him offer evidence as some kind of legal expert of the foundation in law of the Variant A and B document which he admitted that he never saw at the time, only when he was interviewed by the OTP in 2004.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Should we hear it in the absence of witness, Ms. Edgerton, or would it be okay to continue? Just a second. I'm asking Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Rather than continually interrupt the proceedings this morning, maybe it would be better and more efficient to deal with this in the absence of the witness once and for all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kapetina, if you could excuse yourself for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, this man was inspecting how the Defence entities were operating and how they kept custody of the plan. So he was controlling the legality of all the documents and enactments adopted by these organs. So this is matter of fact. This is not a matter of expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you ask the witness about the manual he wrote or the Variant A and B in which he was not involved at all?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked him about Variants A and B, whether it was in line with the law, because it was his duty to supervise whether the companies and other entities adopted contingency plans. He was entitled to go and to inspect the documents to review them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he participate in drafting variant A and B?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so, but he recognised that as an expert work. If I may remind you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a -- what was he at the time? Could you remind us again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was the Chief Inspector of the Ministry of Defence in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He inspected the procedures of preparing for emergency situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just first in response to this last answer that Dr. Karadzic has given. In fact, the witness is not clear on what his duties were at the time the Variant A and B document was issued. He talks of being marginalised by Mr. Doko in March of 1991. He talks of being put at the disposal of Mr. Simovic, and then in March or April of 1992, he talks about finally leaving the Ministry of Defence, but he's referred to documents which at the same time show that he's carrying out tasks for the Serbian Assembly. So his actual duties are completely unclear. And with respect to what's gone on earlier, I do apologise, Your Honour, for what -- my repeated interventions over the course of the morning, and Your Honours have acknowledged some measure of deficiencies in the notice that we've been given. I've raised the question or the issue of the untranslated document, but, Your Honour, I would say that what we're now doing actually compounds the prejudice that we're working under when it comes to dealing with the document. Dr. Karadzic in his questions are taking the situation one step further by having this gentleman comment as a legal expert on a document which he previously hasn't seen before, and I think that's inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think that the question that was asked by Dr. Karadzic could be rephrased, because to ask about a foundation in law seems to invite an expert opinion which this witness is not here to give, but I think given what the role of the witness played in the drafting of this manual and in the Defence preparations, he can be asked how these Variant A and B tallies with the preparations that had been made by the SFRY organs without giving any kind of expert opinions just as, for example, Prime Minister Djeric could be asked on -- as a Prosecution witness about things that he didn't participate in but how it related to the actions of the government. So I don't think there's anything calling for an expert opinion if it's done that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, since everybody gets the chance to stand up today, I guess I'll take the opportunity and simply say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, to be so hurried. I have no idea offhand what analogy Mr. Robinson is attempting to draw between previous occasions when witnesses have been asked about events in which they didn't directly participate, but in this case it is quite clear that the accused is attempting to bridge a factual gap caused by what didn't happen at the time. So he wants to rely on the fact that the witness could have done something that he didn't do, and indeed had the witness engaged in some kind of action at that time it would be sufficiently relevant in this context to elicit, but since that didn't happen, now the accused wants to bridge the gap by either asking for speculation about what might have happened if he did or seeking what is inevitably either an expert opinion on the legality or other aspects of a document which he didn't see at the time or by intruding on the province of the Court by drawing conclusions that fall within the Court's authority. So he's already discussed a document that he participated in and drafted. We have another document before us. The Court will be in a position to make such comparisons and draw such conclusions as may be appropriate. I happen to think this is a bit of a storm in a teacup in any event, but I do draw the line on trying to turn this witness into a kind of expert, in particular given the deficiencies in notice provided to the Prosecution to which the Court has already referred.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I do indeed see this as a storm in a teacup. Is he going to say more than what is contained in para 7, his observation about Variant A and B?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Excellency, given that under item 2 it is said that he was the chief inspector, I may have asked him what was the purview of chief inspector. However, since this paper, Variant A and B, is hugely significant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: His evidence is that he saw that for the first time in July 2004, and he made observation on that document in his statement. I think that's all he can say about this document. Why don't you just move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, this entire manual of his makes it impossible to understand the entire situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's not based only on Variants A and B. It is all based on the local laws and circumstances at a given time. Variants A and B is just a small part. But for this statement not to be too extensive, we wanted this document to be adopted in its entirety because it would help the Chamber understand how things operated in terms of the law. And a comparison also can be made between Variants A and B and the plans that everybody else were obliged to prepare, and as an inspector, it was his duty to supervise it, and there is no better witness to evaluate this paper than this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, now, you did say that the question as structured, it really elicited expert evidence. Fair enough. And you mentioned the way it could have been approached. Can you give us some idea, can you give us some knowledge as to the structure of that particular question you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I had in mind was whether -- was how Variant A and B tallied with the plans that had previously been in place for the SFRY. That's in general. But in discussing with Dr. Karadzic, he, I think, has some very specific questions that might be better put to the witness than on a general level. So perhaps he could explain some questions that he believes he would prefer to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. First of all, I would like to ask the question about the essence of his work. Secondly, who controlled the drafting and drawing up of plans. And thirdly, what was the role in the place of paper A and B even though he hadn't seen it before 2004, but I would like to hear his opinion about its place in the defence system that was in place in the former Yugoslavia. What about Crisis Staff and their place and role, whether they were lawful or unlawful? To put it simply, he was the one who was monitoring the lawfulness of preparations for defence. It was up to him to evaluate this whether it was exaggerated or insufficient and whether it was in accordance with the law. It was his duty from his point of view to assess the lawfulness of these operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, now that Mr. Karadzic -- Dr. Karadzic has given us -- has given us an idea as to the questions he has in mind, do you wish to comment on that please for us so that we have a situation from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, as I see it, Mr. President, I understand that the points that Dr. Karadzic wants to raise and the alleged basis for doing so, he again cites the witness's position at the time, again notes that it had nothing to do with what happened at the time because he didn't in fact know about the Variant A and B document. The alleged credentials he cites for this witness are exactly what a party cites when he wants to explain why someone is entitled to give an expert opinion. So again this emphasises the expert nature of what he is about to ask the witness to do. And interestingly, again, although Dr. Karadzic keeps citing the witness's duty to do this thing, we note that he didn't do it, which seems to underscore apparently the secret nature of the Variant A and B document. But in any event, he has not articulated a basis for doing anything other than attempting erroneously to call this witness as an expert witness to testify about that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the time, the Chamber will have a break. We will resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say just one thing? It would be better to call papers A and B by its correct title, because it speaks about emergency situations. The manual is not a legal text. It just provides guidelines and directions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton and Mr. Tieger, the Chamber has no difficulty with the question suggested by Mr. Robinson and Mr. Karadzic. We will allow the question. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, can you tell us what was the main job of the chief inspector, the job that you had?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: In a nutshell, my main job was to supervise the implementation, the constitution, and the laws pertaining to defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In what way did you discharge these duties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I did it by means of inspection and supervision of planners, mainly the civilian structures of a society starting from state organs at the republican level, then socio-political communities, primarily municipalities and districts, and I also inspected companies that were of special interest for the defence of the republics and other entities in compliance with the inspection plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us if there is suspicion that some organised forces were in the course of preparing violence or rebellions that can precipitate emergencies, what was the obligation of entities involved in that including parties?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Their first task was to make an assessment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Put a pause. Please wait for some time before you start answering the question. The same for you, Mr. Karadzic. Now could you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Their primary task was to continuously monitor the situation and to assess the overall security and political situation in a specific municipality or organ or other planning entity and to define measures that would pre-empt the emergence of such situation or even escalation of certain processes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How is this continuous monitoring being implemented in practice? Are any new procedures being introduced or duty shifts or what? How can you do this on a continual basis?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: This is being done by implementing regular measures but also by reinforced measures. You said yourself that it can take the form of emergency duty shifts or establishing communication and co-operation and checking up. All these measures depended on the decision of a specific planning entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the notion of Crisis Staff, and what can you tell the Chamber about the place of the Crisis Staffs in our system of All People's Defence and civilian protection in general?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Crisis Staffs were not regular organs. As a rule, they were formed on an ad hoc basis depending on the specific circumstances. Mainly those tasks would assume the duties and powers of the regular organs who are failing to carry out their constitutional and legal obligations, and they continue to exist until such time when the regular organs became capable of discharging their regular duties. So as I said, those were not regular organs. Those were ad hoc organs established on a case-by-case basis, and they have a mandate of implementing and using their constitutional and legal powers for a limited period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who made up a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Well, it depends which level we are talking about. If it is on a local level, it depended on the specific situation. In most cases those were members of the leadership who were already holding offices in the existing organs. If we're talking about a municipality, a president of the municipality would be at the head of the Crisis Staff, president of the Executive Committee would be one of the members, and this would also include all those responsible for restoring law and order and suppressing any events that precipitated the crisis by virtue of their office. This could be the chief of police, then the secretary for national defence, perhaps some members of the ruling parties, and that would be the core composition of a Crisis Staff, but it could include other members as well. Basically those were people who held main positions in a local community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The decisions taken by these ad hoc bodies, were they evaluated under regular circumstances? Were they being assessed, adopted, or rejected, which means that the Assembly can only convene after the emergency situation ceases to exist.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes. An Assembly is allowed to evaluate the operation of a Crisis Staff, and it has this power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, at least you should put a pause.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you list us situations in a which a Crisis Staff is established?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: For example, at the local level a Crisis Staff is being formed if regular state organs are dysfunctional. For example, if it is impossible to convene the Assembly or if the Executive Committee is failing to carry out its duties or if any other administrative organs are not functioning. These are the circumstances that call for the establishment of a Crisis Staff, and its main duty is to make the regular organs capable of resuming their duties. Once they achieve that, it ceases to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about natural disasters, accidents, catastrophes other than war? What is the procedure then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: If we are talking natural disasters or large-scale accidents, our system had civilian protection staffs that would then be activated and work to deal with the situation and control the damage caused by a natural disaster or other phenomenon that is a threat to life and property. In such situation a municipality can establish an operative body that is supposed to oversee the situation on the ground and take measures to address the consequences and control the damage caused by natural disasters and other accidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about continuous monitoring? You mentioned duty service. What are the obligations of defence entities in controlling transport, supplying of -- or, rather, monitoring the amount of weapons in circulations controlling entry by unauthorised persons, et cetera. What are their duties in terms of security?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Considering that the defence system in the former Yugoslavia was totalitarian -- or, rather, social, that is to say the entire society was involved in the system, every local community was involved and had the obligation, as well as individuals, to monitor all developments that could threaten peace, order, as well as human lives and property and to report to the competent authorities such as the warning and alert centres and other services whose job was to prevent such threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What are the obligations of defence entities in terms of moving population and property from threatened to safer areas?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: That is only one measure that could be planned. It is known as evacuation. That means moving population and property that could be threatened by a natural disaster, an accident, incidents, or armed activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If a municipality has ten local communes, five Muslim and five Serb, what are its obligations and what can a legal commune legally do in terms of self-organisation and defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: The local commune has its own plan, a contingency plan for natural disasters, accidents and war. In the case of war it would be a defence plan. In the case of natural disasters, that would be another plan. The local commune plans its own forces to implement these plans, but for each measure it has to ask for approval from the higher authority. In such cases a higher authority authorises the enforcement of contingency plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do Defence entities have anything to do with the transport of goods, smuggling, transport of technology, et cetera? Do they have any responsibility to protect citizens in those terms?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Of course contingency plans include such measures as well, but these measures are enforced by the competent authorities, although local communities and citizens may report such things to the competent authorities and ask them to take steps against those who cause trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If there is a danger of war or armed insurgency, what are the competencies of defence entities in terms of movement of conscripts and their travel abroad. Do they have any powers in that field?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Of course, if some measures contained in the plans are ordered to be implemented by the state, then restrictions may be imposed on the movement of conscripts, and they may be required to regularly report to the competent authorities to report their absences and travel but when the competent state body puts in place such a measure or orders the implementation of that plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where are these plans kept? Are they submitted to you or are they kept somewhere, and do you inspect the existence of such plans regularly or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: All these plans are kept by the responsible officer in the entity itself. That is to say, person who manages a particular local body keeps the plan. If we are talking about a political party or a municipality, it would be the president of the Municipal Board of that party who has the plan in safekeeping, and the inspector comes to that person to inspect the plan and the measures contained therein.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What happens if the inspector finds there is no plan?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: If the entity fails to produce the required plan when the inspector comes, then he is subject to penalties under the law, and the person who is the plan manager is also subject to penalties. The person who was supposed to initiate the development of the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you inspect the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: From the establishment of the Ministry of Defence after the first multi-party system, I was not allowed to inspect anything anywhere, including the SDS. To be quite clear, I'm not the only inspector. I am the leader of a team of inspectors from the competent state body. I'm just man number one in the team of inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If an inspection had been made and found that there was no contingency plan in the SDS, what would be the role of the inspector sent by you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: In addition to repressive measures, it's possible that we would talk to the person who was supposed to develop that plan because we don't only have a repressive role but also an instructing role. We have check first whether the dead-line for developing the plan was realistic and reasonable and give a new dead-line. Only if a plan was not made after that second dead-line, then the entity would be subjected to fines and other penalties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In those places where plans do exist, what does the inspection establish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Earlier on the witness said that he was not allowed to inspect anything anywhere, including the SDS. What's the basis of continuing with the witness about the potential inspection vis-a-vis the political parties?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, the witness said that he was prevented from doing that job illegally, that it was an unlawful step taken by the minister. I was asking him what he would have done before he was prevented from doing his job, what he would have done before the minister in question took up that post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm following. Mr. Kapetina, were political parties, including the SDS, the subject of any inspection by your team?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On what basis is a political party subjected to inspection by the government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To give an example: If the programme of inspections envisages an inspection in the municipality, then in that municipality, the inspector would visit one entity in each field, in the industry, in the public industry. They would choose also one political party. It would be a random check, not every entity, just to establish the general picture in that municipality to assess the situation in terms of planning and requirements. To provide a final evaluation of the whole situation in one municipality, it is necessary to cover all planners, all those who have the obligation to have a contingency plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then I'll quote your answer, your previous answer to Mr. Karadzic's question, so could you clarify what you meant. I quote, this is what Mr. Karadzic asked you: "Did you inspect the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party?" Your answer: "From the establishment of Ministry of Defence after the first multi-party system, I was not allowed to inspect anything anywhere, including the SDS." What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I made an inspection plan for 1991 that was not endorsed because the minister of defence is supposed to endorse the inspection plan. I did the same plan for 1992. Again, it was not endorsed. I conducted inspections only before 1990, when there was no Ministry of Defence but the Republic Secretariat for National Defence. So before the multi-party elections I carried out inspections together with my team, but after the multi-party elections I was no longer able to do that because the minister of defence prevented me by refusing to sign the annual inspection plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the reasons why the new minister prevented inspections from taking place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Since in Bosnia-Herzegovina the whole nature of the political system changed from a one-party system - we moved to the multi-party system - there was an urgent need to adapt the defence system to these changes, to harmonise it with new nature of the social and political system. First we introduced amendments on the Law on National Defence and the Law on Conscription, and we needed to develop the bylaws that would allow the enforcement of the laws I just mentioned, but apart from the programmed tasks, the ministry did absolutely nothing. Its staff was busy tearing apart the existing system. They were tearing apart the JNA, tearing the TO apart into ethnic components, and chaos and anarchy, lawlessness were introduced into the system. There were no instructions given to local authorities on how to act. Basically, the ministry did not do the job that it was set up to do, although, as I said, there was an urgent need to work even harder than before because the political system had changed its nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In line 11 you said the minister and the group of people around him. Is that what you said, because it's not on the record?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned a group of people. Those were mainly assistant ministers loyal to the minister from the ranks of the Muslim and Croat communities. Although, even some Croat individuals were not loyal to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that position of the minister in keeping with the law?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Certainly not. His position and his conduct were not in keeping with the law. They were contrary to the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have in evidence an intercept of your conversation with me. Did we know each other before that conversation? Did the SDS make the keeping of your position conditional upon membership in the SDS? Were you a member of any party?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: The first multi-party elections I was a member of the SDP, which was a party that was the successor of the former League of Communists, and I was on the ticket for the local parliament in Hadzici, those elections. Before that conversation, which I believe was in July 1991, I did not know you, nor did you know me. That conversation occurred, as we can see, quite spontaneously, and one of the first things you asked were -- was whether I had to become a member of the SDS in order to keep my job and whether I had to do as the -- whether I had to do the SDS's bidding. Nobody ever imposed any conditions on me, no one and no party. I had worked my entire career in the local administration as a civil servant, and all I did I did in keeping with the powers given me by the law and my workplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In line 17 it says local administration, whereas you said state administration; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I worked in the state administration until 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the first year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Later on when you became part of the Government of Republika Srpska, were any conditions imposed upon you? Did you have to join the SDS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: No. There were no conditions imposed on me that I had to become a member of the party or that I had to carry out any kind of particular party instructions. By way of illustration, in the Ministry of Defence all assistant ministers from the ethnic Serb community who were appointed assistant ministers of defence were not members of the SDS: Ljubisa Terzic, under-secretary, he was not a member; Dragan Markovic was not either; I wasn't; and no one else was a member of the SDS. But we stayed on. We continued to work in these jobs because we were professionals and civil servants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I would like to tender this manual which is quite instructive, and without it it is impossible to understand the civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the actions of various entities. So it's either going to be the translation service or the Defence is going to make sure that all of it is translated and then maybe the Chamber will say that not all of it is needed, but I believe that this manual on action in emergency situations deserves to be part of the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we mark it for identification for the moment and see whether or not to admit it later on, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps only those pages that were referred to in evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was thinking the Prosecution may find some other relevant parts from the document, but if you say so, we'll only mark those pages referred to for identification. Shall we assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be MFI D3860, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had I known, I would have presented more pages, but let's see. Perhaps we'll do it in some different way, bar table it. Thank you, Excellencies. For the time being I have no further questions for Mr. Kapetina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to start, if I -- I'd like to start your cross-examination by looking at a document you've commented about and referred to in your statement. I'll choose P960. And that's the Variant A and B document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I suggest that the witness be given a hard copy of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
