utterances.text: I think the witness will be able to deal with this just fine, Dr. Karadzic, if I go slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But witness was able to follow the document through the monitor. Let's see whether he can follow or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to go over now, Mr. Kapetina, to page 4 in English of this document and page 3 in your language, under the heading "First level," which appears on the previous page, I guess, and instruction number 4. Now, the instruction in this document says: "Convene and proclaim an assembly of the Serbian people in the municipality composed of representatives of the Serbian people in the Municipal Assembly." And just so you know, you found this same passage under the second level of instructions in this document as well, but my question for you is, Mr. Kapetina, since you seem to know something about planning and have looked at this document, maybe you could identify for us the legal provisions, the legal or constitutional provisions that allow a political party to unilaterally create parallel Serb municipality organs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: First of all, I have page 2 on the monitor, and you said page 3, if I'm not mistaken, in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think she was referring to point 4, where it says "Convene and proclaim an assembly of the Serbian people in the municipality ..." Do you see that, Mr. Kapetina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, yes. Paragraph 4, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And do you remember the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I do. I would like to ask you to show the last page of that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Because it will contain -- because it will contain the answer that I'm going to offer to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, why don't you just give the answer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I shall answer instantaneously. In this instruction these are measures and tasks. That is to say that no one ordered this. This -- this was put on a menu, if you will, and for this to be correct, to show that this is correct, do put the last paragraph of this document on the screen for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I do not --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I do not understand why you should see the last page. You cannot answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've answered. This is just a measure that contains the instruction at this level, and this is on the menu for those who are supposed to carry it out. No one ordered this measure. No one from the Serb Democratic Party said: "I hereby order that an Assembly of the Serb people be proclaimed," et cetera, et cetera. That's why I'm asking you for the last page because that is precisely what is written there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question was, Mr. Kapetina, whether it was a menu, order, instruction, whatever it might have been, what's the basis to unilaterally create parallels of municipalities organs. That was the question. I assume that it was not an order at all, instruction. Even it says just suggestion. What's the basis, that was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I will -- well, now was it constitutional and lawful at the level of the republican parliament to out-vote the legally elected representatives of a constituent people? Was that legal? Was that constitutional and lawful?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that your answer, Mr. Kapetina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is just one of the possible reactions at local level. That is to say, when one group of deputies or all the deputies of one constituent people are thrown out of parliament, when you out-vote them with regard to all key questions of national interest, what can you expect from that kind of legally elected parliamentary group? It cannot accept to have someone excluded from political life if they had won the election and evidently they had. So this is just one of the possibilities that was envisaged in the instruction, that this be done at local level, too, drawing on the experience of what happened in the republican parliament. But I note once again that no one ordered this. This was provided as a menu within the instruction, and that is why I'm asking you to show the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will ask Ms. Edgerton to continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to go to actually a different page. No. Actually, it's the same page in English and the same page in B/C/S. Mr. Kapetina, just look down one clause to instruction level -- instruction number 5, and you also find the same passage under the second level of instructions. It says in instruction 5: "Carry out preparations for the establishment of municipal state organs..." and it lists them, "... and prepare a list of nominees for offices and duties in the said organ." And then it says: "Prepare the take-over of staff, buildings, and equipment of security services centres and their integration with the newly established organ of the interior at the seat of the centre." So about this subparagraph or this instruction, I'd like to ask you the same question: Can you identify the legal and constitutional provisions in place in December 1991 that allowed a political party to form, mobilise, and resubordinate a separate Serbian police station and police forces?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: First of all, this instruction does not say that they should be established, these organs. Rather, it says that preparations should be carried out. Do you know that a political party that is in opposition, not in government, can also form a shadow government? They can prepare personnel for setting up a new government. That is the right that a political party has. One that is in opposition, not one that's in government. So these are not documents of establishment. These are documents referring to preparations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kapetina, you can't answer either of my questions, can you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I've answered every one of your questions. You can either be satisfied or unsatisfied with the answers, but I keep telling you that we should look at the last page of this paper, and you keep avoiding that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kapetina, you can't answer my questions because there were no provisions in place at that time that allowed for a political party to unilaterally create Serb municipality and police organs. It's quite simple, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: That is not correct. You are proceeding on the basis of a certain perception. For me members of parliament who were elected to the republican parliament are not a political party, whereas you keep saying that they are the representatives of a party. For me, these are legally elected members of parliament elected by the people. Further on, legally elected members of government, from your point of view they are members of the SDS. From my point of view, in my perception --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if the witness understood the question. Shall we move on?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sure, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact -- so, Mr. Kapetina, in fact you've already said you never saw this document before 2004; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You don't know what happened with this document when it was handed out. You don't know what was said when it was disseminated; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Well, since I am in this field and that I'm professionally linked to this field, I assume what was suggested when it was distributed and distributed down to those who needed --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I didn't ask you for assumptions. I asked you whether or not you knew. Are you now saying that you knew about its distribution and its dissemination?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I can only assume. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine then. We'll move on then to another area. I want to ask you -- I want us to have a look at a document you discussed in your evidence in chief, D3857. So this is a document that was signed by Milan Atlagic, who you said in your written evidence was an associate of yours before he moved to the security unit of the 2nd Military District. So I just want to know is your evidence that Milan Atlagic, who was a career JNA officer, who before he took this job, head of the military police for the military district, was Milan Atlagic passing you strictly confidential military information in February 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Milan Atlagic worked in the sector for security of the Ministry of Defence. His immediate superior or supervisor was Colonel Bjelosevic. Colonel Bjelosevic was assistant minister of defence for security affairs and I was the chief republican inspector. Milan Atlagic did not gather intelligence from the JNA. Rather, he was in charge of security for the civilian sector and the civilian sector of society and that's the kind of information he exchanged with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So let me stop you right there, Mr. Kapetina. My question was is it your evidence that Atlagic was passing you strictly confidential military information, because that's what this document says on the top right-hand and top left-hand corners, was he passing you strictly confidential military information in February 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: In my statement I said that I had not received this information in writing but that I was in a position for Milan Atlagic to provide some information to me of a security nature. Not about the JNA, rather, from the ground, from local communes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that would be a violation of military security on his part, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go over to the second page of this document. Bottom left-hand corner. This document is addressed and only copied to the security organ of the 2nd Military District, the security organ of the 4th Corps, and the security organ of the military district command. Your name isn't there, Mr. Kapetina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I've already said that I had not received information in writing. I repeat that once again. I did not receive this paper. I was in a position to get certain information, security information, from the ground from Colonel Atlagic; that is to say, from municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina and from state organs and so on. I did not say that I had received this information. And now for your information, the command of the military district that Lieutenant-Colonel Milan Atlagic worked in on the 28th of February was beforehand in the sector of military mobilisation affairs of the Ministry of Defence, and it was only later that this was transferred to the command of military district. So the law -- or, rather, the top people in Bosnia-Herzegovina were not in favour of this new organisation that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness start answering from the last sentence. It was too fast for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You were speaking too fast, Mr. Kapetina --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- for the interpreters to follow. So I would like you to kindly repeat from where you said about the law, "... the top people in BH were not in favour...," from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't want to accept the new solutions in the amendments in the law on military obligation, that carrying out military obligation in the republic should be carried out by military territorial organs where this Colonel Atlagic worked. That is the command of the military district. According to the previous law, this work was done by the Ministry of Defence and the municipal secretariats for national defence. Therefore Milan Atlagic was a colleague of mine. Say in this period we were on the same floor in the Ministry of Defence, and we were acquaintances and colleagues, and we had the same work.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to jump over in your statement now to a little bit of your work history in the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska. It seems from your statement you're a pretty long-standing employee because you worked with General Subotic, General Kovacevic, Mr. Ninkovic, General Milovanovic, and it was under General Milovanovic that you also severed as a deputy defence minister for a period, I think; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: In 1997 I was elected deputy minister of defence, and at that point in time Milovanovic was not minister of defence. It was Milan Ninkovic. I did not work in the Ministry of Defence of the Government of Republika Srpska during the term of office of General Manojlo Milovanovic. And what you mentioned here that I worked with Subotic, Kovacevic, and Ninkovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then you were military advisor to Mr. Parvas who was the Serb member of the Bosnian Presidency for a period of time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was advisor for security and defence of the member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Until what point?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: From 2002 to 2006, that term.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And now you're a businessman; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Well, I work in a company. I wouldn't say that I was a businessman.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you're involved -- the company's work is selling arms -- exporting arms and ammunition out of Bosnia and Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes. Beforehand I worked in that company. Yes. That company had a licence and a certificate for exporting arms and military equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So clearly you were a valued member of the defence staff having been in office for so long. You've got some long-standing experience in defence matters. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I think the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in July 1995 when Mr. Ninkovic, who was your minister at the time, was out on the western front, you then were the most experienced official in the defence ministry. You were the most experienced guy left in office; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Well, if we take into account the other assistant ministers, then, yes, I was secretary of the ministry. There were also, say, five or six assistant ministers who also had experience in state administration and the system of defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to get to the point in your statement now where you talk about being called to Dr. Karadzic's office sometime between the 5th and the 10th of July. Now, you had -- did you have your office downstairs in -- in Dr. Karadzic's building or were you in a separate building where the rest of the ministry officials were housed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I was in a different building where the Ministry of Defence of the Republika Srpska was housed, and that was in the Famos factory. I was not in the same building as the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And at that time, just to sort of set the stage for this, at that time his office was on the second floor of the building, and it was kind of down the corridor and on the left-hand side; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: You mean the office of the president of the republic?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I really don't remember. It was possible that it was on one of the stories. It's been a long time ago. I really don't know remember whether it was on an upper floor or on a ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It doesn't really matter. In any case, if Dr. Karadzic needed you, you could be there quickly; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you didn't need a formal appointment to get there either. He could just pick up the phone and call who he needed from your ministry or you, and it was your job to get there as quick as you could; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Right. Of course, this was done through the secretary, not by the president himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when you go up to see him on that occasion in his office, your evidence is that he knew something was going on about Srebrenica, but he didn't know what; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: My impression was that he had received some information but that he didn't have reliable information as to what was actually happening around Srebrenica. In other words, according to the president's conduct, I understood that the information that he received was not the information that he got from officials of Republika Srpska but, rather, from members of the international community, hence he wanted someone to paint a clear picture to him regarding the situation in and around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, talking about his conduct, can you show us or at least describe in more detail exactly how Dr. Karadzic pulled his hair out, knocked over a chair, kicked and knocked over chairs and a table, and asked who the idiots were who ordered Srebrenica? Can you show us or at least describe it more detail?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Well, exactly what you said in your question. In a word, he was furious for not having been informed about anything, primarily by his associates, and he did exactly how I described it. He was kicking a stool, an armchair. He was pulling his hair out. Quite simply he couldn't -- he couldn't accept not to be informed about something that his associates were obliged to inform him about. That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said he inadvertently kicked. What is this called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A stool.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He inadvertently kicked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you pull your hair how the, that's going to cause a great wound, isn't it? It's something you do with great force. How did Dr. Karadzic do it? I want you to show us.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Well, he wasn't pulling his hair out literally. You may have noticed that during all this time here that since Mr. Karadzic has long hair he sometimes put his fingers through his hair, but according all his body language and gestures, I understood that he was infuriated for not having received the information from those who should have provided it to him. That was my point.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's talk a bit more about his body language. And I actually want you to look at a photograph for us. It's P4560. And it's photograph -- it's page 1 of P4560, and it's a photograph of Dr. Karadzic in his office in the Famos factory on the 13th of July, 1995. So there's Dr. Karadzic in his office, and he's there, Mr. Kapetina, with Srdjan Trifkovic, and there's a table in front of Dr. Karadzic with a bowl of fruit on it and some flowers. So when you say Dr. Karadzic knocked over a table, was it this heavy meeting table that he and Mr. Trifkovic are sitting at in his office? What's funny about that, Mr. Kapetina, because that's your evidence in your statement, so I want to find out how it happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I don't think that I said in my statement that he knocked the table over. Maybe a chair or a stool. The table was never mentioned. If that was included in my statement, I should have corrected it. There was no mention of any table.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your statement at paragraph 43 says: "This answer of mine further infuriated the president so that he knocked over a chair, kicked and knocked over some seats, and a table, pulled his hair out, and asked aloud, 'Who needs this right now? Who ordered it? Who are these idiots?'" That's what your statement says. So did he knock over a table or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: No, and that's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance? There is no mention of a table in the Serbian version. Can we please see the relevant paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we take a look at para 43 of his statement. We have no clue other than having to ask the witness to read out the first sentence of para 43.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read the first sentence very slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "This response of mine made the president of the republic even more infuriated so that he overturned a chair. He kicked and turned over a suite, a chair again, he pulled his hair out and asked a question out loud: 'Who needs this at this point in time? Who ordered this? Who these are idiots? Haven't I told you 100 times that the status of Srebrenica has to be resolved within the framework of an overall solution for the BH and that no offensive measures should be taken towards the safe haven?'" So there was no mention of a table. After such a long time I cannot be sure whether the president received me in the office of the president of the municipality. I think that when he asked me over, he was in the offers the president of the municipality, because looking at this picture that was not the office at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So we have a problem with the English translation. That's one thing. And you're now adding to your statement saying that Dr. Karadzic didn't receive you in his office but in the office of the president of some municipality. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: No. In the office of the president of the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh. So now Dr. Karadzic called you about Srebrenica from Mr. Krajisnik's office. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, that would be correct. After having seen this interior and this office, I realise that that was not the office where he received me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when Dr. Karadzic called you from -- was Dr. Karadzic in the habit of calling you from Mr. Krajisnik's office?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: If they happened to be together in either of the office, it made no difference where he would ask me to come over, but in most instances he asked me to come to his office.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So Mr. Krajisnik would have been there then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who else was in the room, in Mr. Krajisnik's office, when Dr. Karadzic called you from that location to ask you about Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: There was no one else. President Karadzic and I were the only people, and there were two secretaries in the adjacent office.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you would have had to go through the secretaries to get to Mr. Krajisnik's office.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Probably. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. Now, let's go back to the picture we had on the screen, P4560. Page 1. All right. Now not accepting for the moment that the meeting happened in Mr. Krajisnik's office, I just want to ask you about furniture. When you say Dr. Karadzic kicked and knocked over chairs, was he kicking and knocking over these leather-bound office chairs that you see he and Mr. Trifkovic sitting on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I said that he did it inadvertently because he was so agitated and nervous that he was walking around the office and waving his hands, so in the process he knocked over a chair. He turned over a stool. And I wrote all this down in order to describe the state of mind that the president was in. I wanted to depict to you his state of mind at the time when he asked me to come over to speak to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So we went from him being so furious that he was ripping his hair out and forcibly turning over the furniture in whatever office you met him in to him running his hands through his hair and inadvertently knocking into furniture; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I have to reiterate that one the chairs definitely was turned over. Whether this was intentionally or intentionally, but I think that it doesn't affect the reason why I went there and why the president asked me to come over.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when Dr. Karadzic said to you or asked you who the idiots were who ordered Srebrenica, that must have been some kind of a trick on his part; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Well, I never talked to the president by using tricks. At least I was convinced of that. I only had serious talks with the president. I never used any tricks, nor do I believe that the president ever treated me unfairly. I am sure that all our conversations were serious, relating to the situation and to our business and our tasks, and I don't think that the president acted by using tricks. He never treated me in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, he must have been deceiving you then, Mr. Kapetina, because when he spoke in public at the opening of this trial, he said: "All of a sudden it turns out once all soldiers enter Srebrenica that they had left Srebrenica. That's when I ordered them to enter the town, to restore peace and order. I have a letter to that effect, because General Tolimir says that's what I actually ordered?" So he must have been deceiving you because it was him all along, Mr. Kapetina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I'm going to object to that. The statement and the testimony has been that somewhere between the 5th and 10th of July this conversation to place, and she's now referring to some event that happened later than the 10th of July. So I don't believe that it's a fair question to imply that Dr. Karadzic is deceiving him based on that example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure when you said some event that happened later than the 10th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The entry into Srebrenica, what she just described in her question. Those events took place after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the date of Mr. Tolimir's report or letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: This was a very late evening of the 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it's between the 5th and the 10th, so I don't see any difficulty with the question. Why don't we continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kapetina, what I put to you was that Dr. Karadzic must have been deceiving you, then, because in public he said he ordered them to enter the town to restore peace and order, and he said he had a letter to that effect because General Tolimir says that's what he actually ordered.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I intervene. Firstly, in line 16 the witness said that I never treated others as well in the same way. Secondly, the witness should be made aware of the difference between ordering and consenting. And also in page 62 it should be explicitly said which soldiers are we talking about, which soldiers entered Srebrenica and which soldiers left Srebrenica. I'm sure that this is an error in the transcript. I am sure that Ms. Edgerton spoke correctly, but it seems that it was not recorded as it should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Probably, Ms. Edgerton, you could read the citation again to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Just your indulgence for a moment. I'll read it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The citation comes from transcript page 982, lines 7 to 10, and the citation is: "All --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's Mr. Karadzic's opening address?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "All of a sudden, it turns out, once all soldiers enter Srebrenica, that they had left Srebrenica. That's when I ordered them to enter the town to restore peace and order. I have a letter to that effect, because General Tolimir says what I actually ordered." Now, Mr. Kapetina, you've had a lot of time to think of an answer to this question, so can we hear it? Was Dr. Karadzic deceiving you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, or rather, the president of the republic, would invite me only in a situation where the minister of defence was absent. He always called me when it pertained to my purview. Since I knew that on that particular day the minister of defence was not at Pale, I believe that President wasn't deceiving me. First of all, I don't know which date it was exactly. It may have been the 5th of July, and I believe that that was the sole reason why the President called me, because he couldn't establish communication with the commander of the Main Staff, the chief of the staff, or any responsible person on the Main Staff who could give me accurate information, and that was the only reason why he called me to come to his office. He asked me if I had any information, not information on my own but information that I had received from either state or military organs, and that was the only reason why he asked me to come over, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, you say you gave evidence that he asked you: "Who needs this right now? Who ordered it? Who are these idiots? Didn't I tell you a hundred times that the status of Srebrenica should be dealt with within the overall solution in Bosnia-Herzegovina and not to take any offensive operations in relation to the safe areas?" Mr. Kapetina, either Dr. Karadzic was lying to you, or when he gave his opening address which was carried in the media around the world he was lying to the public. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. That -- I -- that's a question that falls into the category of when did you stop beating your wife. I don't think that it's an either/or. It can be others -- other explanations as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So now you were told about Mr. Karadzic's opening speech in this trial. Do you still stand by what you said in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully stand by what I said in my statement, and Madam Prosecutor misread my -- his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down. We cannot keep up the pace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton misread what? Could you repeat from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The President didn't use the singular. He used plural. He said, "Didn't I say 100 times at official meetings." He didn't say anything to me personally, because I didn't undertake any actions with regard to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, if I may say, the sentence from the opening statement was misrecorded. I didn't use the word "enter suddenly" talking about soldiers, but when soldiers left Srebrenica, this is what's creating this confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That does not make much difference. Let's leave it. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, you've just said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I was afraid that the transcript was not working, but it's okay. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I do realise we're over time, though, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have long, some more?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we have a break?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will resume at 1.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kapetina, just when we broke before lunch, in the context of talking about paragraph 43 of your statement, you told His Honour Judge Kwon that you stood by that evidence, and what I want to do now, picking up from your assertion, is I want to show you three documents, and then I'm going to ask you a question. The first document is D2097, and it's a report of the Main Staff of the Bosnian Serb Army, dated 6 July 1995. I'm sure there's an English translation, so we'll just wait a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Great. Thank you. Could we please go over to English page 4 and B/C/S page 3, section 6(b), which says: "In reference to the situation in the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps, units of the corps are at the required level of combat readiness. The forces have been prepared and grouped for active combat operations towards the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa and on receiving an interim report will inform you of the combat results achieved so far." Now, if we could go over to page 1 of both these documents, the English and the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Kapetina, that among all the other recipients of this VRS Main Staff daily combat report, the president of the Republika Srpska is listed first; right? If you see that, and then we're going to leave this document and go on to the next one.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I've seen it. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thanks. Now I'd like us to have a look at D02080. It's an interim combat report from General Krstic, dated 9 July 1995, to the VRS Main Staff, and it says at paragraph 3 under the heading "Decision for further operations." "Taking advantage of the success achieved, regroup the forces and carry out a vigorous and decisive attack towards Srebrenica." So you see that; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to tell you what Dr. Karadzic said about this document in this trial, and that's from transcript page 27725, testimony dated 20 April 2012, and it's referring to July 1995, the same date of this document. Dr. Karadzic said: "Do you remember that on that day it was in the evening, after 2220," that's 10.20 p.m., "General Krstic informed the main staff that he had the opportunity of liberating Srebrenica, of entering Srebrenica, and a half hour later Tolimir sent a telegram back to him with my approval?" Right. Now I want to show you the document from General Tolimir, and then I'll ask you a question. And that document from General Tolimir is P2276, dated 9 July 1995, and it's an order from General Tolimir, and it's copied to Dr. Karadzic for information, and it's transmitted to Generals Gvero and Krstic personally, and it's about the conduct of combat operations around Srebrenica, and it says: "The President of Republika Srpska has been informed of successful combat operations around Srebrenica by units of the Drina Corps and that they have achieved results which enable them to occupy the very town of Srebrenica." And in the second paragraph it says: "The president of the republic is satisfied with the results of combat operations around Srebrenica and has agreed with the continuation of operations for the take-over of Srebrenica, disarming of Muslim terrorist gangs, and complete demilitarisation of the ... enclaves [sic]." So Mr. Kapetina, when Dr. Karadzic told you that he couldn't establish communication with the commander of the Main Staff or any responsible person on the Main Staff who could give accurate information, that's not true, is it, because these documents show exactly the opposite, these documents and Dr. Karadzic's own words in this trial.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The question is, Mr. Kapetina, that when Dr. Karadzic told you that he couldn't establish communication with the commander of the Main Staff or any responsible person in the Main Staff, that that wasn't true, was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was true or not. Maybe President Karadzic invited me on the 5th of July. You are commenting on something that happened on the 6th or 9th. Perhaps he summoned me on the 5th when he did the not have that information, or perhaps on the 4th. I said roughly between the 5th and the 10th. You're acting like I remember dates. Maybe he invited me on the 5th, and then these reports followed after that on the 6th and 9th. Perhaps they came later. I'm telling you from what I know, from what I heard, and from what I was told at the meeting, that he had no information from the Main Staff, that he was unable to contact the defence minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I didn't object because the question was complicated and I didn't want to disturb the flow, but this is the second time today that the President has used Dr. Karadzic's non-evidentiary submissions as evidence, and I just want to point that out, and I believe that that's not correct, and I just hope that we all have the same understanding. So when he puts a question to a witness in his capacity as self-representing accused, there is no factual assertion there that is evidence either for or against him. Similarly when he made an opening statement, not the personal statement he made at the beginning of the Defence statement but the opening statement at the beginning of the case. That is also not factual assertions as a witness or as a person so that those also cannot be used as evidence. So I hope we all agree on that. Otherwise, it may cause us problems when we're writing our briefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is there anything to comment upon, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, yeah, there is, Mr. President, because I don't agree and I think the Court is aware that we don't. We asked for a warning at the beginning of the case. We made clear our position on that. We were told, I think, as I recall the events, that a sufficient admonition or a sufficient notification of that position had been made clear to the accused. And finally, I would note that in any event, it certainly is sufficient to say it is the position of the Defence or it is the Defence's case that, which is certainly a basis for cross-examination and impeachment by itself. So for both those reasons I cannot agree with Mr. Robinson, and that's why I rose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you agree that part of question or statement does not -- do not form part of the evidence in this case, whether -- separate from whether the Prosecution can use that bit for the cross-examination of other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You can't -- you can't unring the bell in this way, Mr. President. I don't believe the Prosecution could use it as affirmative evidence in the kind of classical way the Court may be indicating, but to demonstrate the position of the parties, to demonstrate the position of the accused in certain instances to the extent it may be relevant in assessing the evidence, I think it's certainly appropriate to use, and it can play a very significant role in the case, but -- so we may -- it sounds like we don't have a disagreement, but I was concerned about the -- what I would regard as an attempt to ignore completely such assertions in court for all purposes, and I think that would be inaccurate and unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, now, you're now saying that you actually weren't sure of the date of this meeting, that it could have been on the 4th or on the 5th or any time up to the 10th, but -- and, Mr. Kapetina, in your evidence today at page 56 of the temporary transcript, you said that the meeting was arranged by the secretary, and I had a look, Mr. Kapetina, at Dr. Karadzic's appointment calendar for that period of time, July 1995, part of which you saw at paragraph 4367. And the whole appointment calendar, for the record is P2242. Mr. Kapetina, for the period between the 1st and your meeting on the 13th of July, 1995, your name doesn't appear in Dr. Karadzic's engagement calendar. That's because this meeting where the chairs were knocked over never happened; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: That meeting happened, and I noted down exactly what transpired at that meeting. I had a feeling that the president was calling me urgently through the secretary. It's not the kind of appointment that you note down in the appointment book or in the protocol log. The secretary made an urgent call to me and told me to see the president. I told you before it's possible that this was also in the office of the speaker of the Assembly. There was no prior appointment. It was ad hoc. What would have happened if I hadn't been in my office? Then the meeting would have never happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have one last question before we go on to another area, a brief area, and it's about the date of this meeting that you keep going back and forth on, Mr. Kapetina. Mr. Kapetina, the evidence in this case is that the attack on Srebrenica didn't commence until 4.00 in the morning on 6 July 1995. All right? And that's the same date as the report to Dr. Karadzic that I showed you when we began this session, D2097. So I want to come back to this, Mr. Kapetina. You keep waffling about the date, but you continue to assert that Dr. Karadzic didn't have contact with the Main Staff. Now hearing the Prosecution's case and the evidence that the date of the attack is on the 6th of July, do you still stand by your statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I emphatically stand by what I wrote in my statement and the evidence I gave in answer to your two questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. Then I just want to go on to one final area from your testimony, and that's - your indulgence for a moment - with respect to paragraph 45 where you talk about the mobilisation by the Ministry of Defence of buses for the army. And you said at paragraph 45 that whether the army was planning to transport its own forces to another theatre of war or for other purposes, the Ministry of Defence didn't have to know this. So I just want to ask you, Mr. Kapetina, that's not what the buses your ministry was mobilising were for, was it? You were mobilising them to remove the non-Serb population from Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I was not at the ministry when that order and that request arrived from the Main Staff. You see that the order was signed on behalf of assistant Kovacevic by his employee. I said in my statement that the responsibility, regardless of the purpose for which the trucks and buses were commandeered, lies with the Ministry of Defence because we are duty-bound to meet the request of the Main Staff and provide the resources regardless of the purpose for which the army is going to use them. That's what I said in my statement. And if I had been at the ministry, since the minister was away, I was the one who would probably have signed this request for mobilisation. But I wasn't there. You see that somebody -- not even the assistant minister signed it. It was some senior employee.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was whether you agreed that the buses were mobilised to remove the non-Serb population from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: No dispute. Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When, actually, did you find that out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Well, I found out from the media reports, television reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When, actually, did you find that out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact date, but I learned that from the media reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the most senior official in the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska whose department was specifically responsible for the implementation of the military request to mobilise buses to remove the non-Serbs from Srebrenica, and you only found out from the news reports and you don't know when. That's your evidence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: That's precisely my answer to your question. And let me correct you, I was not in charge of mobilisation. It was assistant Kovacevic. At that time, I was a secretary of the Ministry of Defence. I did not have a specific portfolio. I was a secretary in the Ministry of Defence in charge of regulations, statutes, bylaws, whereas there was a specific portfolio called mobilisation and staffing. Let me tell you about other things that I knew and didn't know about. I saw directive number 7 only yesterday. At that time I never knew such texts were drafted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, feel free to tell Dr. Karadzic those things in his redirect examination of you, but my time allotted for your cross-examination is up, so thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kapetina, let's start with the last thing in the cross-examination. Was that the first and the only mobilisation or, rather, commandeering of transport vehicles requested by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I believe that requests for additional manpower and assets came from the army every week. It was a continuous job at the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we put this document on the ELMO if it hasn't been uploaded. This is 11 January 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you just read these few sentences beginning with "I hereby order."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: "Immediately mobilise all motor vehicles, socially and privately owned, with a capacity of over 7 tonnes. "2. All motor vehicles of the said carrying capacity must report together with the drivers without delay to the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska at the petrol station Podromanija Sokolac to the dispatcher."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it say for which purpose?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document to be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely not, Your Honour. It's -- it's -- it's -- the witness has just read the document out and absolutely nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How does it relate to the cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was suggested that a high official of the ministry must have known for what purpose motor vehicles were mobilised in July 1995. We see here that this was a frequent occurrence. The witness said almost once a week. And the purpose is not indicated. It was not the duty of the Main Staff or the ministry to specify the purpose. This follows directly from the suggestion made by Ms. Edgerton. The witness said -- the transcript is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is incorrect, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has been corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't think I suggested anything of the sort, Your Honour. All I did was to reference the witness and the Defence to what the question was, which was what -- what the buses were mobilised for. I read out his own evidence at paragraph 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we look at line 4 of page 75, the question she put was: "Was this the first and only mobilisation or, rather, commandeering of transport vehicles requested by the Main Staff?" So this goes directly to that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's Dr. Karadzic who said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber does not think this is relevant. We'll not admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then I'm not going to show a couple of more documents that relate to the mobilisation of motor vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, do you know how many rooms there are around my office and whether I always received people in the same room, that is to say in my office, rather than any of the adjacent rooms?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Of course you received people in adjacent rooms. I don't know how many there were exactly at that level, but I know there was a conference room, and sometimes you would receive people in the conference room too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at D02080 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us to whom is this addressed, this interim combat report? Did it reach me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this is addressed to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you look at the passage in paragraph 2 -- item 2, paragraph 3, it says: They ... "carried out the immediate task separating the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica and created conditions for extending the attack towards Srebrenica." Were you aware of their immediate task to separate Zepa and Srebrenica, and were we entitled to do that according to the agreement on those two protected areas?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I did not know about any task that had to do with Srebrenica or the surrounding area. However, as far as I know about the principles of protected areas, I think it was legitimate for the Army of Republika Srpska to have a buffer zone between these two enclaves and the UN protected areas, because it was well known in the area of Zepa, that was a far bigger area, air supplies came of ammunition and weapons and so on and units in both protected areas resorted to that, and I think this was a legitimate activity because they were treated as two separate protected areas not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who stopped our army in 1993, stopped it from entering Srebrenica, and for what reason?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not relevant with respect to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, on the day when you saw me and when I complained that I did not have any information, at that point in time did I know that the 28th Division had left Srebrenica and that they would not defend it? Did I inform you about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: You did not inform me about anything. You just asked me to, I mean, say whether I had any information and whether I had received anything from the Main Staff or the Drina Corps. At the end you just apologised to me. I mean, because you were arrogant in the way you were addressing me, but it didn't really have to do with me. It had to do with the entire situation and the people who were supposed to be doing their jobs. That is how you had put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I wanted to link it up that way because the Defence position is that the assumption was that there would be heavy fighting and -- Srebrenica, I would not have given consent to enter Srebrenica, but that is the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have the opportunity to testify about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us -- could you please tell us, on page 53 you said -- it was suggested to you that military secrets were being revealed to you. Can you tell us which defence and security measures and information should be concealed from the chief inspector of the minister of defence on the ground? Is it a military secret. I mean anything that comes from the ground, is that a secret for the chief inspector?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Military secrets only have to do with JNA units and information in the army, whereas in the Ministry of Defence the ministry is a civilian organ, a state organ, and state secrets were the most restricted secrets, highly confidential, confidential, and restricted. And then information about personnel capacity within the military, within units, that was military secrets, whereas we in the state organs had state secrets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us about that example -- or, rather, that copy of Atlagic's report, did it stay in the archives of the ministry? All the addressees were referred to, but such matters -- I mean, were copies left at the ministry too?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Well, I think there were, unless their assessment was at that point in time that it should not be sent to the ministry, but it should be in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was suggested that there were no legal grounds for establishing a Serb municipality, taking measures, and so on, so could we please have -- could we please have in e-court 1D9735. Now there's an MFI number, 1D1935.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, I didn't make that suggestion at all. What I asked was for Mr. Kapetina to identify the specific legal and constitutional provisions which permit a political party to establish separate Serbian municipalities. Which he did not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll get to that too. Page 8, please. The page where number 8 is written. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please listen to this. I'm going to read this out. This comes from the Law on National Defence, and you refer to it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot find this passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the third paragraph, Excellencies. It's the quotation within the third paragraph. Oh, yes. Oh, I see, we don't have a translation here. All right. So then it's paragraph 3, and then quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could Dr. Karadzic put a question rather than reading -- leading the witness by reading a document that we can't read.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the question is the one that was put by Ms. Edgerton: Where are the legal grounds for papers A and B, legal and constitutional grounds?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why can't you ask the question without showing the document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then I'm going to ask for Variants A and B. P5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think P5 is a different document. P960.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all the same, any number. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, the first sentence. Could you take a look at the first sentence. And could we please have the next page in English. Could you tell me what does this sentence stem from, and what is your association in respect of regulations? The first sentence.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Well, this is an assertion to the effect that the constitutional order of the country is under threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now go back to the previous document. What is envisaged in that kind of situation when the constitutional order of the country is under threat?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: To declare a state of emergency and to implement plans for stopping or eliminating emergencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1D9735, page 8, paragraph 3. The quotation there, that is precisely what he said, but we've got it again now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, Your Honour, but this is not matter arising from the question in cross-examination, which was whether or not the witness can identify, as I said, the provisions that allow for the creation of separate Serb municipal organs. If he can, then Dr. Karadzic can ask him that question and he can answer it now rather than be led through documents in a way that I would submit isn't permissible in redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think Dr. Karadzic could show the witness a document and ask him to comment on it as to whether -- how or whether it in fact shows that such a provision was in existence. So I don't think there would be anything improper if he has such documents or if he knows of them to ask the witness to comment on whether or not those documents confirm the existence of the right to do what they purported to do under Variants A and B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the basis for the question that Madam Edgerton put with regard to municipalities. Can you say on the basis of the constitution how are municipalities created, or, rather, what do municipalities consist of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: A municipality consists of local communes as basic cells of the society, and the municipality is territorial government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Local communes, do they have the right to leave one municipality and join another one or to turn themselves into a separate municipality? How are new municipalities created according to the law?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: On the basis concrete examples that happen in this period I will explain this. Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 had 109 municipalities and the city of Sarajevo as a community of several municipalities, and say before that, a year before that, the municipality of Pale separated itself from the city and became a municipality outside the city. So it is sufficient to launch an initiative within the local Assembly and then to create, say, two municipalities out of a single municipality if necessary, and there can be different reasons: Economic development, ethnic structure, joining a different district or city or whatever. There can be many reasons. For example, before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Bijeljina was supposed to be divided into two municipalities, Bijeljina and Janja, and the procedure had already started, and we know that the Muslim population there had already asked for a municipality of their own because that would guarantee faster economic development.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You confirmed during the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination that the local commune has some authority with regard to defence. Can you tell us on the assumption where we have a municipality with five Serb local communes and five Muslim local communes, what are the powers of the five Serb local communes if they assess that the other five municipality -- the other five local communes are threatening the constitutional order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is over the top I would submit, Your Honours. It's not arising out of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Tieger. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was only going to say in addition it has nothing to do with the Variant A and B document which is why I presume the accused didn't take the witness to the document. So it may have been obvious to the Court based on its own familiarity with it, but we've now strayed beyond the terms of that particular document into some -- a new area. So it wasn't simply that it wasn't triggered by Ms. Edgerton's specific question. It wasn't even triggered by the subject matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My problem is this: The witness was not able to answer your question, Ms. Edgerton, as to what the basis was with respect to instruction, Variant A and B, and in re-examination for the purpose of refreshing the memory or whatever, Mr. Karadzic was showing some documents, and then can you not hear what the witness would say after having taken a look at the document? Is there --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just -- if I just -- I know you're asking Ms. Edgerton so I apologise, but since I was -- I was on to a particular subject matter. That -- but not if it's no longer about A and B, which is not about the alleged legal basis for the establishment of -- by local communes of new municipalities. It's about, as the Court is aware, some of the other specific matters that -- to which the witness's attention was drawn during the course of the cross-examination. So now Dr. Karadzic is using the cross-examination about the document as a basis for moving into a separate area of interest to him but that did not arise out of cross, pretending somehow it's related to the Variant A and B document when it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Actually, what -- we do not know what is cited in this document. We haven't heard about it, whether it's related to it or not. Mr. Kapetina, could you read out aloud what is contained in the inverted commas in the sentence with the footnote number 2. From "Pod drugim." Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Read please slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "According to the law on All People's Defence, emergency situations are defined as follows: 'For the purposes of this law, other emergency situations shall denote armed or other activity directly threatening the independence of the country, its sovereignty and territorial integrity and the social order established by the constitution of the SFRY.'" That is a quotation from the Law on All People's Defence of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, can you tell us what is the relation between this quotation and the quotation from A and B on item 1 that you saw at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina does not know much about Variant A and B document. How can he say about the relation? So why don't you move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Excellencies, Mr. Kapetina's job was to check how preparations were going on including organisations such as SDS. I'm asking him whether this was within the confines of the law or outside the confines the law. That was his job to know. We may ask him is there anything contained in this paper that is not stipulated by the law?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Move on, Mr. Karadzic, to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, can you tell us is there anything in the regulations that gave the right to Serbian local commune to reorganise themselves or to self-organise themselves in terms of establishing their own municipalities and their own authority?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: We have already established --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We collapse this document. And your question again, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What the Serbian local communes undertook or the Serbian territorial units such as municipalities and local communes, was that stipulated by regulations that govern emergency situations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes. Not only Serbian local communes but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, Dr. Karadzic keeps going outside of the bounds of the cross-examination, and he's doing it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We're simply wasting some time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Excellencies, the question was on what basis the Serb municipalities were established, and I'm asking Mr. Kapetina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just directly put the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The creation of Serbian municipalities, was that possible under the law and the constitution, particularly in terms of emergency situations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: In peacetime the procedure of establishing a municipality or the division of municipality was regulated by the law. Under the emergency circumstances, one has to act according to plans and instructions, and an instruction in my view is just part of the plan. Tasks and measures that are contained in an instruction cannot be treated as part of the law or the constitution, because it's a plan, and it needed to be ordered to become an action, but I didn't see any such order. That's why it says that such measures need to be specifically ordered either by the party or by the state, and the party can issue such an order only if it is endorsed by the state, and that's what it says at the end of the instruction, i.e., that none of these measures were ordered and each of these measures required a separate order, and I myself never saw such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So drawing up a plan, does that imply its automatic implementation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. It depends on a specific situation. You might draw up a plan that would never materialise. It might just act as a deterrent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, you were asked about the legal foundation, the constitutional foundation of certain procedures. Can you tell us about the rights of those involved in the defence when you have a destroyed legal and constitutional system? Are there any provisions stipulating the rights and obligations under such circumstances, whether you have the country under an occupation or in any other situation where there is no constitutional system in existence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: The period between January --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honour. Same objection. Provisions stipulating rights and obligations whether you have a country under occupation. This is far and away outside anything raised in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless you have any further topics, I would like you to conclude your re-examination, Mr. Karadzic. It leads us nowhere.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. My understanding of disputing the issues raised in cross-examination was that this witness did not confirm the legality and lawfulness of the acts of the Serb side, whereas I claim the opposite and it is contained in his manual as well, and with this I'm going to conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Kapetina. Thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the next witness ready, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It would be good if we can start him since he's been waiting a long time today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness will be Professor Radovan M. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Karadzic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good luck to you, President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you given a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In future, I would kindly ask you to pause before answering so that everything can be recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D9683 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see your statement on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it, and I've signed it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see the last page so that the witness can identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect the answers that you gave to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does faithfully reflect what I told the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today in this courtroom, would your answers essentially be the same?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: They would be the same. Only in the interests of the truth and nothing but the truth, I might make some additions in terms of additional facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement into evidence under 92 ter Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Pack?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3681, Your Honours. I apologise, D3861.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it should be 3881. Thank you. Now I'm going to read a summary of Mr. Radovan M. Karadzic's statement in English. [In English] Radovan Karadzic, son of Marko, was a teacher of literature in Capljina in the former BH until the beginning of the war when he was expelled from the place where he lived and worked. During the period from 1990, Professor Karadzic -- until Professor Karadzic was expelled from Capljina in April 1992, he was the president of the Capljina SDS Municipal Board, president of the Serb Municipal Assembly in Capljina, president of the Capljina Crisis Staff, member of the Serb National Council for Herzegovina. After his arrival in Pale in April 1992, president of the Presidency, Karadzic, appointed Professor Karadzic as an advisor for internal politics and party issues. Professor Karadzic was also a member of the SDS Main Board. He knows President Karadzic since he was a child, and he remembers him to be exemplary in every respect. President Karadzic was among the best pupils in school and the most prominent student in his generation and later an excellent doctor. President Karadzic spent his youth and a great deal of his life in Sarajevo, a Muslim-Serbian city. He studied with Muslims and later he worked and lived as their neighbour. Professor Karadzic never heard him saying anything that would indicate intolerance towards the Muslims. The SDS was envisaged to be an entirely democratic and to a great extent decentralised party. President Karadzic did not interfere in personal matters.
